marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q015.takeaway: Thyroid gland extends approximately from C5 through T1.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q015.displayText: The extent of the thyroid gland is from vertebral levels A to D in the source image, corresponding to C5 to T1.

rationales.a: B–D would stop too high and omit the upper cervical-to-thoracic extent shown.
rationales.b: A–C is shorter than the labeled gland extent.
rationales.d: C–D would omit upper cervical levels; source maps full gland from A to D.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q016.takeaway: Thyroid isthmus usually overlies second to fourth tracheal cartilages.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q016.displayText: The structure marked X is the isthmus of the thyroid gland. It overlies the 2nd, 3rd and 4th tracheal rings. The isthmus connects the lower parts of both lobes and is usually anterior to the 2nd and 3rd tracheal cartilages, though its position may vary with size.

rationales.a: Third through fifth tracheal cartilages shift the isthmus one ring too low.
rationales.b: First and second rings are too superior; source places it over rings 2–4.
rationales.d: Third and fourth rings alone omit the usual second-ring coverage.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q017.takeaway: Inferior thyroid artery runs near recurrent laryngeal nerve; branches should be controlled near gland.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q017.displayText: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is related to the posterior branch of the inferior thyroid artery near the thyroid lobes. Therefore the artery is ligated close to the gland to prevent nerve injury. The external laryngeal nerve is related to the superior thyroid artery; the superior thyroid artery is also ligated close to the gland to avoid injury to that nerve.

rationales.a: Superior laryngeal nerve is related to superior thyroid artery; inferior thyroid artery dissection risks recurrent laryngeal nerve.
rationales.c: Glossopharyngeal nerve does not run with inferior thyroid artery at thyroid bed.
rationales.d: External laryngeal nerve is related to superior thyroid artery, not inferior thyroid artery.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q018.takeaway: Inferior thyroid artery branches from thyrocervical trunk.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q018.displayText: Inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.

rationales.b: External carotid is the head/neck artery from which superior thyroid arises, not the inferior thyroid artery.
rationales.c: Internal carotid gives no cervical branches.
rationales.d: Lingual artery is an ECA branch; inferior thyroid arises from thyrocervical trunk.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q019.takeaway: Superior/middle thyroid veins can admit air during neck surgery under negative pressure.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q019.displayText: The scenario is suggestive of cerebral air embolism. Intra-operative injury to the superior or middle thyroid veins can allow air to be sucked in because of negative venous pressure. The embolus travels via the internal jugular vein into cerebral venous circulation. Head-down position during surgery prevents air embolism. Superior and middle thyroid veins drain into the internal jugular vein; the inferior thyroid vein drains into the brachiocephalic vein.

rationales.b: Inferior thyroid vein is part of midline surgical field, not the described venous air-entry route through superior/middle thyroid veins.
rationales.c: Superior and inferior thyroid vein pairing is inaccurate; source associates cerebral air embolism with superior or middle thyroid vein injury.
rationales.d: Thyroid arteries carry arterial blood and do not provide the venous route for air embolus.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q020.takeaway: Berry ligament anchors thyroid to cricoid cartilage, causing movement with swallowing.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q020.displayText: Movement of the thyroid gland with deglutition is due to the attachment of Berry's ligament to the cricoid cartilage. The pretracheal fascia forms the false capsule and thickens posterolaterally as Berry's (lateral thyroid) ligament, attaching the posteromedial thyroid lobes to the side of the cricoid cartilage. It also prevents the thyroid from sinking into the mediastinum.

rationales.a: Thyroid gland attaches to hyoid via fascia/muscle relationships, but Berry ligament inserts on cricoid.
rationales.c: Berry ligament attachment is to cricoid cartilage, not tracheal rings.
rationales.d: Thyroid cartilage is not the insertion specified for Berry ligament; cricoid fixation moves gland with swallowing.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q021.takeaway: Inferior thyroid artery is lateral, while isthmus/ima artery/inferior thyroid veins lie near midline tracheostomy.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q021.displayText: The inferior thyroid artery is not damaged during emergency midline tracheostomy because it is not a midline structure. The thyroid isthmus, arteria thyroid ima, and inferior thyroid vein are in the midline and are prone to injury.

rationales.a: Thyroid isthmus is midline and can be injured in emergency tracheostomy.
rationales.b: Arteria thyroid ima, when present, is a midline vessel at risk.
rationales.d: Inferior thyroid vein crosses midline and may be injured; inferior thyroid artery is lateral.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q022.takeaway: Parathyroids receive supply from superior branches of inferior thyroid artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q022.displayText: The scenario suggests postoperative hypoparathyroidism due to injury to the superior branch of the inferior thyroid artery. Parathyroid glands are small yellowish-brown structures between the posterior border of the thyroid gland and its capsule. There are two superior and two inferior glands. They are supplied by the superior branch of the inferior thyroid artery and secrete parathormone.
emphasis: superior branch of the inferior thyroid artery

rationales.a: Superior thyroid artery supplies superior pole but source identifies inferior thyroid artery branches as principal parathyroid supply.
rationales.b: Posterior branch of superior thyroid artery is not the keyed vessel supplying parathyroids.
rationales.d: Inferior branch of inferior thyroid artery is not the superior branch specified in this source.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q023.takeaway: Sternothyroid attaches to thyroid cartilage and helps limit upward thyroid swelling.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q023.displayText: Sternothyroid and sternohyoid prevent upward extension of thyroid swelling through attachment to the thyroid cartilage. Pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid and attaches to the larynx, producing movement with deglutition. The thyrohyoid membrane is fibro-elastic, arising from the superior margin of thyroid cartilage and attaching to hyoid bone, facilitating upward laryngeal movement during swallowing. Berry's ligament extends from cricoid cartilage to thyroid and prevents the gland from sinking into the mediastinum.

rationales.a: Pretracheal fascia encloses thyroid and attaches to larynx but is not the strap muscle resisting upward expansion asked.
rationales.c: Thyrohyoid membrane connects thyroid cartilage to hyoid, not a muscle.
rationales.d: Berry ligament tethers thyroid to cricoid, but sternothyroid attachment to thyroid cartilage is the selected structure.

marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q024.takeaway: Proposed tubarial glands lie near torus tubarius on lateral nasopharyngeal wall; evidence and “new gland” status are still discussed.
marrow__ANAT_CH31_Q024.displayText: The newly discovered salivary glands are predominantly present over the torus tubarius, the anatomical structure formed by cartilage supporting the entrance of the auditory tube. The proposed name is tubarial salivary glands. They extend caudally to the pharyngeal wall and cranially to Rosenmuller's fossa. PSMA PET/CT can visualize these glands with high sensitivity and specificity. Radiotherapy over their location has been reported to cause xerostomia and dysphagia; sparing them might improve quality of life.

rationales.a: Soft palate is not the location named in descriptions of tubarial gland clusters.
rationales.c: Posterior tongue is not their reported nasopharyngeal site.
rationales.d: Auditory tube is adjacent, but the source places the proposed glands over the torus tubarius; this item’s “newly discovered salivary glands” label is a terminology claim, not a new anatomical landmark.

reconstruction.sourceProblem: The source presents tubarial salivary glands as newly discovered, while subsequent anatomy studies discuss whether they represent a distinct major gland versus previously recognized nasopharyngeal gland clusters and report low functional salivary-gland mass contribution.
reconstruction.reconstructedContent: The newly discovered salivary glands are predominantly present over the torus tubarius, the anatomical structure formed by cartilage supporting the entrance of the auditory tube. The proposed name is tubarial salivary glands. They extend caudally to the pharyngeal wall and cranially to Rosenmuller's fossa. PSMA PET/CT can visualize these glands with high sensitivity and specificity. Radiotherapy over their location has been reported to cause xerostomia and dysphagia; sparing them might improve quality of life. The source-keyed site remains torus tubarius; “newly discovered” refers to the proposed named tubarial gland complex and should not be read as denying pre-existing descriptions of local mucous glands.
evidenceBasis: Anatomy ED8 source explanation and key, q24, pp. 552–553.
